newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German region makes progess in sick pay row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German region makes progess in sick pay row.

text.p: German regional trade union officials in the south-western state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said on Monday they had agreed to enter wider talks with engineering employers to find a solution to a bitter dispute over sick pay.

Gerhard Zambelli, regional head of the IG Metall metal and engineering union, said after initial talks with employers that any agreement found in the regional talks could later be used as a "pilot agreement" elsewhere in the country.
"We need a solution somehow and we're trying to get one," Zambelli told journalists in the Black Forest town of Freudenstadt. Further talks have been set for November 7.

Baden-Wuerttemberg, home to Daimler-Benz AG's Mercedes car-making unit, has been one of the areas hit hardest by worker protests against a new law cutting sick pay allowances from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
Around 800,000 of the metal and engineering sector's 3.5 million workers are employed in the region.
The regional talks in Freudenstadt were the first to take place in the metal and engineering sector since since national-level discussions collapsed last week.

Those talks broke down as trade union negotiators refused any cut in sick pay while employers federation Gesamtmetall insisted that such cuts were necessary within the 1997 wage agreement for the industry.

But Dieter Hundt, chief negotiator for the employers' side, said after talks on Monday that both sides agreed that the regional discussions set for November should not be "a simple repetition" of the earlier negiotiations.

Signs of an early breakthrough had already emerged as trade union officials said there was a "strong chance" of a deal on the employment protection measures that the union is demanding for inclusion in new regional contracts.

Job creation and protection measures forms the main part of IG Metall's 1997 wage demand announced earlier this month. Agreement there could pave the way for a possible compromise on the cost-cutting measures such as the sick pay reductions.
Hundt had said before going into talks that the employers would be ready to make compromises, but only if IG Metall changed its position.
Baden-Wuerttenberg along with the North-Rhine Westphalia steel-making region were the two areas worst hit by walk-outs involving hundreds of thousands of workers last week.

An earlier day of protest by workers this month forced major companies including Daimler to postpone plans to implement the cuts until wider agreement on wages and labour costs had been reached with the union.
IG Metall and Gesamtmetall had met for two days of talks to attempt to resolve the dispute last week but talks broke down with both sides accusing the other of intransigence.

Gesamtmetall said after the collapse of discussions that issues such as sick pay would now most likely have to be solved on the regional level -- a development widely seen as harmful to the future of the German system of collective bargaining.
Worker and employer representatives in other industries such as the chemical sector are still attempting to find agreement on the sick pay issue at the national level.
